caption:
Nvidia has told its cloud partners to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, the Financial Times reported.
The rule covers new contracts. Nvidia's top chips cannot ship to China, but Chinese firms can still rent them through clouds abroad.

Will this slow down China's AI labs?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

threads_text: Nvidia reportedly told cloud companies that at least 51% of their sales must go to non-Chinese customers. Its best chips cannot ship to China, so Chinese firms have been renting them through clouds abroad. Will this actually slow China down?

site_article.headline: Nvidia tells cloud partners to keep Chinese customers below half of sales, FT reports
site_article.dek: The reported rule applies to new contracts and targets a common way Chinese firms reach Nvidia's most advanced chips: renting them from data centers abroad.
site_article.summary: Nvidia has told cloud providers that use its chips to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, the Financial Times reported on November 3, 2026. The requirement covers future contracts and was passed on verbally, according to the report.
site_article.seo_title: Nvidia tells cloud partners to cap Chinese sales below 51%
site_article.seo_description: Nvidia reportedly requires cloud partners to sell at least 51% of services to non-Chinese firms on new contracts, the Financial Times said.
site_article.answer_summary: According to the Financial Times, Nvidia now requires cloud companies using its chips to sell at least 51% of their services to customers outside China on new contracts. Nvidia has not confirmed the report.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia has told the cloud companies that rent out its AI chips to sell at least 51% of their services to customers outside China, according to a Financial Times report published on November 3, 2026. The newspaper cited five people with knowledge of the matter. AFP, Techzine and Yahoo Finance each summarized the report the same day.

According to the report, the instructions were passed on verbally by Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams in recent months rather than in formal written documents. Techzine noted that Nvidia had not previously placed any conditions on where its cloud partners' customers come from.

The requirement applies only to future contracts and does not affect existing lease agreements, the reports said. Two of the sources told the Financial Times that it covers all of Nvidia's cloud customers worldwide, not only data centers in Asia.

Yahoo Finance pointed out that the report describes a cap on the share of business a provider can do with Chinese companies, not a ban. Chinese customers could still use Nvidia powered cloud services, as long as they make up less than half of a provider's sales.

Washington has restricted sales of certain high performance chips to China since at least 2022, and Nvidia's most advanced processors cannot be shipped there directly. Many Chinese companies instead lease capacity from data center operators abroad for demanding work such as training AI models, Techzine reported.

Chinese technology firms are major buyers of AI computing capacity in Southeast Asia, so operators there would need to find other clients. A Singapore based group told the Financial Times that it is hard to find enough non-Chinese customers outside the United States. One person familiar with the market said a rack of Nvidia B300 chips that costs about $600,000 internationally recently sold in China for the equivalent of $2.8 million.

The move follows other steps around Nvidia hardware in 2026. Earlier in the year, Nvidia reduced the number of Asian companies authorized to buy its advanced chips, according to Techzine. Yahoo Finance noted that several senior Super Micro employees were charged this year over the alleged smuggling of about $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI servers to China; the charges are allegations and do not establish guilt.

Nvidia neither confirmed nor denied the report to AFP. In a statement, the company said that data centers and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide, and that America cannot win the AI race unless its AI infrastructure wins worldwide.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of the report. She added that Beijing hopes all parties can provide a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for companies from every country, including Chinese firms.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the reported rule shifts the chip contest from shipping to renting. Export controls already block Nvidia's best hardware from entering China, but rented capacity abroad has remained a practical route. A sales cap enforced through Nvidia's own commercial relationships would narrow that route without any new government regulation, and it puts the burden on cloud operators in places like Southeast Asia to change who they serve.
The next thing to watch is whether Nvidia confirms the requirement in writing, and whether cloud operators in Southeast Asia report slower sales or turn away Chinese clients on new contracts.
